# Hydrometallurgical process for recovery of metal values from spent nickel-metal hydride secondary batteries

Pingwei Zhang a,b,), Toshiro Yokoyama b, Osamu Itabashi b, Yoshito Wakui b, Toshishige M. Suzuki b, Katsutoshi Inoue c

Japan Science and Technology Corporation, Japan

Received 27 February 1998; revised 2 June 1998; accepted 8 July 1998

## ABSTRACT

A completely hydrometallurgical process has been developed for the recovery of metal values such as cobalt, nickel and rare earths from spent nickel-metal hydride Ni-MH secondaryŽ. batteries. Effects of hydrochloric acid concentration, temperature, reaction time and solid-to-liquid ratio on leaching of metals contained in the electrode materials of the batteries were studied. The optimal operating conditions were found to be 3 M HCl at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C and a 3-h leach time, and it was possible to treat up to 5.5 g of scrap in 50 ml of acid solution where the recoveries 100% of cobalt, over 96% of nickel and 99% of rare earths were achieved. A typical chemical composition of the resulting leach liquor was approximately, in grams per liter, 23.4 Ni, 1.7 Co, 3.4 Fe, 0.72 Zn, 0.46 Al, 1.2 Mn, 4.2 La, 0.26 Ce, 0.82 Pr, 2.6 Nd and 0.074 Sm, as well as 50 Cl. The pH of the solution was around 1.2. The rare earth values can be readily recovered from the leach liquor by the use of a solvent extraction circuit with 25% bis 2-ethylhexylŽ. phosphoric acid D2EHPA in kerosene, in which a two-stage counter-current extraction at an O:A Ž. ratio of 3:1 at an equilibrium pH of 2.0, a single-stage cobalt scrubbing with 0.3 M hydrochloric acid at an O:A ratio of 22:1, and a stripping operation with 2.0 M hydrochloric acid in one contact at an O:A ratio of 5:1 are involved. A mixed rare earth oxide of over 99% purity was obtained by selective precipitation with oxalic acid, and calcination of the precipitate. The total yield of rare earths approached 98%. The cobalt and nickel in the raffinate are effectively separated by selective extraction of cobalt with 25% TOA in kerosene after concentration up to ClŽ w yxf220 g y1 l. Nearly complete recovery of cobalt can be achieved by using a three-stage counter-current.

extraction at an O:A ratio of 2:1, followed by stripping with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution Ž. pH 2.0 in a single stage at an O:A ratio of 4:1. Subsequently the cobalt in the strip liquor and the nickel remained in the raffinate are separately recovered as oxalates by the addition of ammonium oxalate. A pure cobalt product and a nickel oxalate with a purity close to 99.9% were obtained. The total recoveries of cobalt and nickel were found to be approx. 98% and 96%, respectively. q 1998 Published by Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

Keywords: Nickel-metal hydride; Cobalt; Hydrochloric acid

## 1. Introduction

Interest in the recycling of used household batteries such as alkaline, zinc–carbon, mercuric oxide 1, lead 2,3 and nickel–cadmium Ni–Cd 4–7 batteries has in-w x Ž. w x creased substantially in recent years, primarily for environmental reasons. At present, the reclamation of nickel-metal hydride Ni-MH battery alloys is also receiving increasingŽ. attention 8–10. In the authors’ previous publication 11, a hydrometallurgical processw x w x for the recovery of cobalt and lithium from spent lithium-ion secondary batteries was described. The current paper reports the separation and recovery of metal values such as nickel, cobalt and rare earths from spent Ni-MH secondary batteries.

The Ni-MH battery has a structure similar to that of the Ni–Cd battery. It is tightly sealed to prevent the leakage of electrolytic solution and the generated gas during charging. The positive electrodes are constructed of a porous Ni plate with nickel hydroxide as activating agent. The negative electrodes consist of a hydrogen storage alloy powder such as Mm–Ni–Co MmŽ. sMisch metal on a metal-mesh substrate. The two electrodes are separated by an inert insulating layer. The chemical reactions of the two electrodes can be expressed by the following equations.

The cathodic reaction:

M + H2O + e ⇌MH + OH ^- (Eq. 1)

The anodic reaction:

Ni (OH)2 + OH ^- ⇌NiOOH + H2O + e (Eq. 2)

The overall reaction:

Ni (OH)2 + M ⇌NiOOH + MH (Eq. 3)

where the forward direction is the charge reaction and the reverse is the discharge reaction. M represents the alloy to be hydrided.

The Ni-MH batteries possess several advantages 12 over other batteries such as the w x Ni–Cd rechargeable battery: 1 higher electrochemical capacity 1.5–2 times the Ž. Ž Ni–Cd battery; 2 long charging–discharging cycle 500–1000 cycles; 3 wide. Ž. Ž. Ž. temperature range (- 20 to + 60 ^∘C) Ž.; 4 lower self discharging rate and a wide range of material selection; 5 safety and acceptability towards the environment. No hazardousŽ. Ž materials are used, such as cadmium and lead which are utilized in the Ni–Cd and Pb batteries, respectively..

Ni-MH batteries were developed in 1989 and commercialized in 1990 in Japan. As described above, since use of Ni-MH electrodes offers enhanced electrochemical properties in many instances as well as reduced environmental toxicity, in recent years batteries utilizing Ni-MH electrodes have been used extensively in portable electronic applications including the personal computer, video-recorder and telephone, and so on. The throughput of Ni-MH batteries approached 18 million units in 1992 and about 70 million units in 1993 in Japan, and the estimated consumption in the year 2000 will cover approximately 50% of the market. The lithium-ion secondary batteries willŽ probably share 30% and Ni–Cd batteries 20%. Additionally, because of their high. energy density and design flexibility, Ni-MH batteries are particularly well-suited for battery powered electric vehicles EV and other mobile applications. Consequently, it Ž. can be predicted that an appreciable amount of spent Ni-MH batteries will be generated in the near future. The expected tonnages of both primary and secondary scrap are potentially very large. Recycling of these batteries after use has thus become an important issue. From the point of view of the economic incentive, the Ni-MH batteries contain a variety of valuable mineral resources like nickel, cobalt and rare earths, etc. In addition, recycling will be significant due to the likelihood that the environmental regulations for nickel may become more stringent. The purpose of this research was to develop an effective hydrometallurgical process for the separation and recovery of metal values such as nickel, cobalt and rare earths from spent Ni-MH secondary batteries. The overall experimental approach used was to leach the internal components in hydrochloric acid followed by metal recovery using different techniques including solvent extraction and precipitation.

## 2. Experimental

## 2.1. Materials

The Ni-MH batteries used in this work were cylinder-shaped batteries TOSHIBAŽ TH-3A type. The commercial extractants employed, bis 2-ethylhexyl phosphoric acid. Ž. Ž. Ž. D2EHPA was kindly donated by Daihachi Chemical Industry and trioctylamine TOA was purchased from Aldrich Chemical Company Inc. These reagents were utilized without any further purification. The concentrations of the extractants in the organic solution were 25% by volume. The diluent was kerosene. 1-Dodecanol was used as third phase inhibitor in the TOA system, and its concentration was 15 vol.%. The organic solution of TOA was pre-equilibrated by contacting with twice volume of 2 M hydrochloric acid solution for 10 min before the extraction experiments. Other reagents were of analytical reagent grade quality.

## 2.2. Experimental procedure

## 2.2.1. Demolishment of batteries

The nickel-metal hydride batteries were cut in half longitudinally to separate the metallic cases from the internal battery rolls which consisted of the positive and negative electrodes plus a nylon separator. The cells weighed an average of 24.8 g each and contained an AB5 - t y p e rare earth metal system negative electrode. The weight of theŽ. positive electrode in one cell was 7.27 g and that of the negative electrode was 10.57 g in which the alloy powder accounted for 87.6% and the metal-mesh 12.4%. The components of the active material on the positive electrode, the alloy powder and the metal-mesh on the negative electrode were determined separately by total dissolution with aqua regia.

## 2.2.2. Leaching studies

Leach tests on cells were carried out using hydrochloric acid solution. In each test, 3.08 g of battery scrap which consisted of 1.25 g of the positive electrode materials and 1.83 g of the negative electrode materials were leached in 50 ml of HCl solutions of suitable concentrations in a 100-ml beaker under electromagnetic stirring, except for the tests on the effect of solid-to-liquid ratio on the leaching of metals. After leaching, the leach solution and insoluble residue were separated by filtration. The concentrations of each metal in the leach solutions were measured.

## 2.2.3. SolÕent extraction studies

Extraction and stripping tests were carried out batchwise by contacting suitable volumes of the organic and aqueous phases in a 50-ml centrifuge tube or a 500-ml separatory funnel at ambient temperature (25 ± 0.5 ^∘C). The pH was adjusted by the addition of a concentrated sodium hydroxide solution to the appropriate value. From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium. The extraction and stripping kinetics of cobalt with TOA were very rapid. The time for reaching extraction equilibrium was less than 5 min, while the stripping occurred almost immediately after the loaded organic phase was contacted with a stripping agent. Neither a third phase nor an obvious change in volume of the two phases was observed in all cases. After the two phases were disengaged, the aqueous phase was taken to determine the pH and the concentrations of the metals.

## 2.2.4. Precipitation of rare earths

The mixed rare earths were precipitated from the strip liquors of the extraction circuit with D2EHPA by the addition of concentrated ammonia solution until a pH 2–3 was reached, followed by an excess of saturated oxalic acid solution about 2 mol Ž rmol of rare earths. The mixture was heated and stirred for ca. 1 h, and the precipitated rare. earth oxalate was filtered, washed with hot water, and dried in air. The oxalate was calcined in a muffle furnace at 850 - 900 ^∘C to convert it to a mixed rare earth oxide product.

## 2.2.5. Precipitation of cobalt and nickel

The cobalt and nickel were precipitated from the strip liquor and the raffinate from extraction circuit with TOA, respectively, by the addition of ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions. The precipitates were dissolved with small amounts of concentrated sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid solutions and diluted with water to determine the contents of impurity elements.

## 2.3. Analysis

The concentrations of metals in both initial feed and equilibrium aqueous solutions were determined by inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectroscopy using a SEIKO SPS 1200A ICP-AES spectrophotometer. Those in the organic phase, in principle, were calculated in accordance with mass balance, unless otherwise noted. The total concentration of rare earths, which is represented by RE in the text, is thew x summation of the concentrations of individual rare earth elements in the solution.

The chloride ion concentration in the aqueous solutions was determined gravimetrically by silver chloride precipitation.

## 3. Results and discussion

## 3.1. Determination of the battery electrode materials

The chemical constituents of the positive and negative electrodes were analyzed by total dissolution with aqua regia. The results are given in Table 1. It can be seen that the positive electrode was composed basically of nickel and small amounts of cobalt and zinc. The amounts of iron, aluminum and manganese were less than 0.2% by weight. On the other hand, the negative electrode consisted mainly of nickel, rare earths, iron and cobalt. The other metals zinc, aluminum and manganese accounted for less than 6.4%.Ž. Further analyses for the alloy powder and the metal-mesh on the negative electrode showed that the iron stemmed essentially from the metal mesh. The content of iron in Ž the metal mesh was 88.5% and that of nickel was 10.9%. The alloy powder was.

[TABLE:TABLE_Hydrometallurgical Process for Recovery of Metal Values from Spent Nickel-Metal Hydride Secondary Batteries_0001]

composed mainly of nickel and rare earths as well as a small amount of cobalt which accounted for 54.1%, 34.5% and 3.6%, respectively.

## 3.2. Leaching studies

The effect of four variables, viz., HCl concentration, temperature, reaction time and solid-to-liquid ratio on metal leaching was studied.

The relationship between the percentages of metals leached and the HCl concentration is shown in Fig. 1. The leaching of metals was found to depend highly on the HCl concentration at [ HCl ] < 2 mol l ^-1. Nearly complete dissolution occurred for all metals when the HCl concentration approached 3 mol 1 ^-1. However, there appeared to be a slight decrease in the percent of the rare earths leached when the HCl concentration exceeded 4 mol 1 ^-1

Fig. 2 illustrates that the leaching of iron is affected significantly by temperature. At low temperature, for instance, at 35 ^ ∘C, the percent leached could only reach about 40%, whereas this value would be increased with the increase in temperature, reaching completion at 95 ^ ∘C. It appears that the leach efficiency of nickel was less dependent on temperature at < 65 ^ ∘C, where the percent of nickel leached was kept at approximately 87 %. However, when the temperature was allowed to continue to rise, the leaching of nickel increased. Almost total dissolution was accomplished at 95 ^ ∘C.. The leaching of other metals was far less dependent on temperature over the temperature range examined. Essentially complete leaching could be achieved at 35 ^ ∘C for cobalt, rare earths and aluminum and at 55 ^ ∘C for zinc and manganese.

The time dependency of the leaching of metals with 2 M HCl solution at 95 ^ ∘C is given in Fig. 3. Apparently, the leaching of cobalt, aluminum, manganese and rare earths proceeded very rapidly, reaching completion in less than 15 min for aluminum and manganese and less than 30 min for cobalt and rare earths. On the other hand, the relatively slow leaching of iron, zinc and nickel, especially the latter, was observed. The complete leaching was achieved in about 1, 2 and 2.5 h for iron, zinc and nickel, respectively.

The effect of the weight of scrap on the leaching of metals is shown in Table 2 in terms of the percent recovery of metals in the leach liquor. Overall, low scrap weight gives high leaching yields of metals, whereas increasing the proportion of scrap leads to incomplete leaching, particularly nickel. The effect of scrap weight on leaching of rare earths seems to be insignificant within the experimental range of scrap weights studied. However, the use of excessively small amounts of scrap is evidently undesirable from the point of view of maximizing metal concentration in the leach liquor and minimizing the lixiviant consumption. Accordingly, the suitable scrap weight was considered to be 5.5 g in 50 ml of acid solution.

[TABLE:TABLE_Hydrometallurgical Process for Recovery of Metal Values from Spent Nickel-Metal Hydride Secondary Batteries_0002]

Based on the above experimental results, the final optimum conditions for leaching were determined to be 3 M hydrochloric acid, a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:9 at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C for 3 h. Under these conditions, 96% of nickel, > 99 % of rare earths and 100% of cobalt could be leached. At the same time, however, the other impurity elements were also nearly completely dissolved in the solution. The average composition of the resulting leach liquor was found to be approximately, in grams per liter: 23.4 Ni, 1.7 Co, 3.4 Fe, 0.72 Zn, 0.46 Al, 1.2 Mn, 4.2 La, 0.26 Ce, 0.82 Pr, 2.6 Nd Ž and 0.074 Sm total RE 7.95 gl ^-1). The chloride ion concentration was 50 g1 ^-1 and the pH was about 1.2.

## 3.3. RecoÕery of rare earths

3.3.1. Separation of impurities and rare earths from cobalt and nickel by solÕent extraction with D2EHPA

Investigations into the use of acidic organophosphorus reagents for the solvent extraction of metal ions from aqueous solutions have shown that D2EHPA in organic diluents can be highly loaded with divalent transition metals like Cu ^2+ [ 13 - 17 ], n ^2+ w x 13,16,17, Cd ^2+ w x 15,17, Zn ^2+ w x 2q w x 13,15–17, Co 13,14,16–18, Ni ^2+ 13,14,16,17.w x Moreover, the extractability sequence from chloride medium can be written as Zn ^2+ > Mn ^2+ > Cu ^2+ > Cd ^2+ ≈ C ^2+ > Ni ^2+ 13,17. D2EHPA also exhibits a powerful extrac-w x tion for trivalent metal cations like Fe ^3+ [ 19, 20 ] and Al ^3+ [ 21 - 23 ]. The pH1 / 2 values Ž. defined as the pH at which 50% metal extraction occurs for Zn ^2+, Mn ^2+, F⃗ ⃗e⃗ ⃗^⃗3⃗+⃗ 24, w x Al^3+ 25 lie below pH 3, whereas those of cobalt and nickel are 4.08 and 4.52 24,w x respectively. These data demonstrate the possibility of removing impurities from cobalt and nickel by the use of extraction with D2EHPA at low pH. On the other hand, it is well known that D2EHPA shows an excellent extraction behavior towards trivalent rare earth elements in weakly acidic solution 26,27, and undoubtedly still forms the basis of w x several commercial processes for the separation of these metals 28. Fortunately, thew x separation of the rare earths from these impurities can be achieved by means of selective precipitation with oxalic acid as will be described later.

Fig. 4 gives the results for the extraction of zinc, aluminum, iron, manganese, cobalt, nickel and rare earths with 25 vol.% D2EHPA in kerosene from the actual leach solution mentioned above at various pH values. It is clear that the rare earths can be quantitatively extracted and separated from cobalt and nickel at pH-2.2. However, as expected, under these conditions, nearly complete extraction of aluminum and iron as well as about 85% extraction of zinc takes place. Above pH 2.0, the extraction of cobalt begins to occur. It is noteworthy that, according to the reported data 12,17, manganesew x should be extracted to a considerable extent at pH close to 2. Nevertheless, it can be seen from Fig. 4 that a large amount of rare earths and other impurities such as iron, aluminum and zinc prevent manganese from being taken up into the organic phase, since D2EHPA can extract these metal ions more strongly than manganese. The resulting effect is that only a very small amount of manganese Ž.; 15% is transferred to the organic phase. Hence, it is necessary to increase the organic-to-aqueous ratio and use a multistage extraction operation in order to eliminate manganese completely from the solution. For this reason, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of manganese from the leach liquor by 25% D2EHPA in kerosene was constructed by contacting the two phases at various phase ratios at an equilibrium pH 2.0. The equilibrium data are presented in Fig. 5. The McCable–Thiele diagram indicates that essentially complete removal of manganese can be achieved in two counter-current stages at an organic-toaqueous phase ratio of 3:1. The aqueous feed liquor was therefore processed in a two-stage batch counter-current experiment over six cycles, using 240 ml of organic phase and 80 ml of aqueous phase for each contact. The equilibrium pH for each contact was adjusted to 2.0 with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. The raffinate obtained after a six-cycle operation, where steady-state conditions had been reached, showed the presence of 0.005 g l ^-1 of manganese. The concentrations of zinc and aluminum were, in g1 ^-1, 0.09 and 0.002, respectively, while those of iron and the rare earths were below

0.001 gl ^-1. The extraction of cobalt was less than 13%, whereas nickel was not extracted at all. The incomplete extraction of zinc is probably attributed to complexation of zinc ion with chloride ion 13,15,29.w x

## 3.3.2. Scrubbing of cobalt from the loaded organic phase

The small amount of cobalt co-extracted into the organic phase was easily removed by scrubbing with 0.3 M HCl solution at an O:A ratio of 22:1 in a single stage. The scrub solution contained, in gl ^-1, 1.70 Co, 1.63 Mn, 0.042 Zn, 0.010 Al and 0.013 La. No iron and none of the other rare earths was detected in the scrub solution. This solution was returned to be mixed with the leach liquor.

## 3.3.3. Stripping of rare earths

Table 3 gives the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration and of organic-to-aqueous ratio on the stripping of metal ions from the organic phase. It was found that the rare earths could be stripped readily using a hydrochloric acid solution of appropriate concentration ca. 1–3 M. The somewhat low recoveries of rare earths at low HClŽ. concentration or at high O:A ratio are due to the incomplete stripping of praseodymium and neodymium from the organic phase. As expected, these rare earths are extracted by D2EHPA more strongly than the lighter rare earths like lanthanum and cerium. Almost quantitative stripping could be accomplished with 2 M HCl solution in a single contact at an O:A ratio of 5:1, thereby giving rise to a strip liquor containing, in gl ^-1, 13.2: RE 0.27 Al, 1.13 Zn, 1.72 Mn, 0.016 Co and 0.02 Fe. Higher concentrations of rare earths could be obtained, if required, by use of a multi-stage counter-current stripping operation at a greater O:A ratio.

[TABLE:TABLE_Hydrometallurgical Process for Recovery of Metal Values from Spent Nickel-Metal Hydride Secondary Batteries_0003]

Additionally it can be seen from Table 3 that the stripping of iron is very poor under the experimental conditions. Nevertheless, further experiments showed that the stripping of iron was enhanced significantly when the concentration of hydrochloric acid exceeded 4 M. The McCable–Thiele plot Fig. 6 shows that a more than 99% stripping ofŽ. iron is theoretically possible using a 6 M HCl solution in four counter-current stages at an O:A ratio of 5:1. Under these conditions, aluminum is also removed completely from the organic phase.

After the stripping of iron, the organic phase is recycled to the extraction circuit for reuse.

3.3.4. Separation of rare earths from impurities and recoÕery of mixed rare earth oxide product

As seen from the above results, since partial stripping of aluminum and essentially complete stripping of zinc and manganese together with rare earths from the loaded organic phase took place, further separation was required to obtain a pure rare earth product. This was achieved by selective precipitation of rare earths with oxalic acid from the strip liquor as described in Section 2.2.4, leaving the other impurities in solution. Calcination of the oxalate gave a mixed rare earth oxide product containing 53.3% La2O3, 3.4% CeO2, 10.5% Pr6O11, 32.1% Nd2O3 and 0.8% Sm2O3. With respect to impurities other than rare earths, analyses for three samples showed them to contain 0.014% CoO, 0.008% MnO, 0.025% ZnO, 0.052% Fe2O3 and 0.56% Al2O3. The loss of rare earths was about 1%.

## 4. Recovery of cobalt and nickel

After removal of rare earths and impurities from the leach solution by extraction with D2EHPA, the remaining raffinate contained cobalt and nickel as well as a small amount of zinc. In order to recover pure cobalt and nickel products, a cobalt–nickel separation was required. It is known that the selective solvent extraction of cobalt from chloride solutions containing nickel using a tertiary amine extractant is being practiced on a commercial scale 30,31. The extraction of cobalt from an aqueous solution with loww x acidity rises with the chloride ion concentration. Substantial extraction of cobalt occurs at [ C ] ^- ] ≥200 g1 ^-1 32,33. Hence, in the present work, the raffinate was concentratedw x by evaporation to reach a chloride ion concentration of about 220 g1 ^-1 before extraction.

Preliminary tests on a concentrated aqueous feed liquor showed insufficient extraction of cobalt in a single contact at unit phase ratio with 25% TOA in kerosene. Accordingly, to achieve quantitative extraction of cobalt, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of cobalt from the concentrated solution by 25% TOA in kerosene was determined. The results are shown in Fig. 7. The McCable–Thiele construction demonstrates that it should be possible to achieve nearly complete extraction of cobalt from a solution initially containing 6.75 gl ^-1 of cobalt in three counter-current stages at an O:A ratio of 2:1. To confirm this, a three-stage counter-current batch simulation was carried out. After nine cycles the representative raffinate was found to contain 0.018 g 1 ^-1 of cobalt corresponding to an extraction yield of > 99.7 %. The loaded organic phase contained 3.37 g l ^-1 of cobalt.

Subsequently the cobalt in the loaded organic phase was stripped by contacting it with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution pH 2.0 in a single stage at an O:A ratio of 4:1. Ž. The stripped organic phase was found to contain only 0.007 g1 ^-1 of cobalt, indicating a stripping efficiency of 99.8%. The strip liquor was a pure cobalt chloride solution containing 13.45 gl ^-1 of cobalt. It should be pointed out, that although zinc has been reported to be extracted from chloride medium by TOA 32,34, no zinc was observed inw x the loaded organic phase in the current work.

The cobalt in the strip solution was recovered as a cobalt oxalate precipitate by the addition of an excess of ammonium oxalate. The percentage precipitation of cobalt was over 98.5%.

The raffinate from the cobalt extraction contained high levels of nickel, together with a small amount of zinc and trace levels of cobalt. The nickel was recovered directly as a nickel oxalate by precipitation with ammonium oxalate. The contents of impurity elements in the obtained products were determined to be 0.004% cobalt, 0.002% aluminum, 0.098% zinc and < 0.002 % manganese. No iron and rare earth elements were detected by ICP-AES. The average recovery of nickel was higher than 99.9%.

## 5. Conclusions

The hydrometallurgical process developed for the separation and recovery of rare earths, cobalt and nickel from spent Ni-MH secondary batteries consists of the following five major unit operations: 1 total leaching of the electrode materials of the batteriesŽ. with hydrochloric acid; 2 isolation of rare earths and impurity elements from cobaltŽ. and nickel by solvent extraction with D2EHPA; 3 selective precipitation of rare earths Ž. as oxalates and separation from impurities; 4 separation of cobalt from nickel by Ž. extraction with TOA; and 5 separate precipitation of cobalt and nickel as oxalates. AŽ. conceptual total flow diagram of the process is proposed Fig. 8.Ž.

The best conditions for leaching were found to be 3 M HCl at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C and a solid:liquid ratio of 1:9 for 3 h. Under these conditions, over 96% of nickel, 99% of rare earths and 100% of cobalt could be leached.

The rare earths and impurities were extracted from the leach liquor with 25% D2EHPA in kerosene at pH 2.0, cobalt and nickel remaining in the raffinate. The loaded organic phase was scrubbed with a 0.3 M hydrochloric acid to remove a small amount of the co-extracted cobalt, prior to stripping the rare earths with 2 M HCl. The rare earths in the strip liquor were precipitated selectively with oxalic acid and isolated from impurity elements such as aluminum, zinc and manganese. After calcination of the precipitated oxalate, a mixed rare earth oxide containing 53.3% La2O3, 3.4 % CeO2 10.5% Pr6O11, 32.1% Nd2O3 and 0.8% Sm _ 2 O3 was obtained. The content of impurities other than rare earths in the oxide product was found to be less than 1%. The total recovery of rare earths reached around 98%.

The cobalt and nickel in the raffinate were separated efficiently by selective solvent extraction of cobalt with 25% TOA in kerosene after concentration ([ Cl ^- ] ≈ 220 g l ^-1) Cobalt and nickel were recovered as oxalates by precipitation with ammonium oxalate and pure cobalt and nickel oxalates with a purity of about 99.9% were obtained. The total yields of cobalt and nickel were approximately 98% and 96%, respectively.

stages.label: Process

records.name: hydrochloric acid leaching of battery scrap
records.evidence_hint: Leach tests on cells were carried out using hydrochloric acid solution. In each test, 3.08 g of battery scrap ... were leached in 50 ml of HCl solutions of suitable concentrations.

records.name: solvent extraction with D2EHPA
records.evidence_hint: Extraction and stripping tests were carried out batchwise by contacting suitable volumes of the organic and aqueous phases ... From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium.

records.name: solvent extraction with TOA
records.evidence_hint: The extraction and stripping kinetics of cobalt with TOA were very rapid. The time for reaching extraction equilibrium was less than 5 min, while the stripping occurred almost immediately after the loaded organic phase was contacted with a stripping agent.

records.name: precipitation of rare earths
records.evidence_hint: The mixed rare earths were precipitated from the strip liquors of the extraction circuit with D2EHPA by the addition of concentrated ammonia solution until a pH 2–3 was reached, followed by an excess of saturated oxalic acid solution about 2 mol rmol of rare earths. The mixture was heated and stirred for ca. 1 h, and the precipitated rare earth oxalate was filtered, washed with hot water, and dried in air. The oxalate was calcined in a muffle furnace at 850 - 900 °C to convert it to a mixed rare earth oxide product.

records.name: precipitation of cobalt and nickel
records.evidence_hint: The cobalt and nickel were precipitated from the strip liquor and the raffinate from extraction circuit with TOA, respectively, by the addition of ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions.

records.canonical_name: hydrochloric acid leaching of battery scrap
records.content: Leach 3.08 g of battery scrap (1.25 g positive electrode materials and 1.83 g negative electrode materials) in 50 mL of HCl solution of suitable concentration in a 100-mL beaker under electromagnetic stirring; after leaching, separate leach solution and insoluble residue by filtration.

Batchwise extraction and stripping tests by contacting suitable volumes of organic and aqueous phases in a 50-mL centrifuge tube or 500-mL separatory funnel at 25 ± 0.5 °C; adjust pH with concentrated NaOH; use 30-min contact time for extraction and stripping equilibria of metal ions, except stripping of aluminum requires about 60 min.

Batchwise extraction and stripping tests by contacting suitable volumes of organic and aqueous phases in a 50-mL centrifuge tube or 500-mL separatory funnel at 25 ± 0.5 °C; adjust pH with concentrated NaOH; extraction equilibrium for cobalt reached in less than 5 min and stripping occurs almost immediately after contacting loaded organic phase with stripping agent.

Precipitate mixed rare earths from D2EHPA strip liquors by adding concentrated ammonia solution to pH 2–3, then adding excess saturated oxalic acid solution (about 2 mol per mol of rare earths); heat and stir for about 1 h; filter, wash with hot water, dry in air, and calcine the oxalate in a muffle furnace at 850–900 °C to convert to mixed rare earth oxide product.

Precipitate cobalt from the TOA strip liquor and nickel from the TOA raffinate by adding ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions; dissolve the precipitates with small amounts of concentrated sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid solutions and dilute with water for impurity analysis.

text_chunk.text:
## 2.2.2. Leaching studies
Leach tests on cells were carried out using hydrochloric acid solution. In each test, 3.08 g of battery scrap which consisted of 1.25 g of the positive electrode materials and 1.83 g of the negative electrode materials were leached in 50 ml of HCl solutions of suitable concentrations in a 100-ml beaker under electromagnetic stirring, except for the tests on the effect of solid-to-liquid ratio on the leaching of metals. After leaching, the leach solution and insoluble residue were separated by filtration. The concentrations of each metal in the leach solutions were measured.

text_chunk.chunk_id: CHUNK_Hydrometallurgical Process for Recovery of Metal Values from Spent Nickel-Metal Hydride Secondary Batteries_2.2.3. SolÕent extraction studies_9173d7eb
text_chunk.text:
## 2.2.3. SolÕent extraction studies
Extraction and stripping tests were carried out batchwise by contacting suitable volumes of the organic and aqueous phases in a 50-ml centrifuge tube or a 500-ml separatory funnel at ambient temperature (25 ± 0.5 ^∘C). The pH was adjusted by the addition of a concentrated sodium hydroxide solution to the appropriate value. From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium. The extraction and stripping kinetics of cobalt with TOA were very rapid. The time for reaching extraction equilibrium was less than 5 min, while the stripping occurred almost immediately after the loaded organic phase was contacted with a stripping agent. Neither a third phase nor an obvious change in volume of the two phases was observed in all cases. After the two phases were disengaged, the aqueous phase was taken to determine the pH and the concentrations of the metals.

text_chunk.text:
## 2.2.4. Precipitation of rare earths
The mixed rare earths were precipitated from the strip liquors of the extraction circuit with D2EHPA by the addition of concentrated ammonia solution until a pH 2–3 was reached, followed by an excess of saturated oxalic acid solution about 2 mol Ž rmol of rare earths. The mixture was heated and stirred for ca. 1 h, and the precipitated rare. earth oxalate was filtered, washed with hot water, and dried in air. The oxalate was calcined in a muffle furnace at 850 - 900 ^∘C to convert it to a mixed rare earth oxide product.

text_chunk.text:
## 2.2.5. Precipitation of cobalt and nickel
The cobalt and nickel were precipitated from the strip liquor and the raffinate from extraction circuit with TOA, respectively, by the addition of ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions. The precipitates were dissolved with small amounts of concentrated sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid solutions and diluted with water to determine the contents of impurity elements.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.2. Leaching studies
The effect of four variables, viz., HCl concentration, temperature, reaction time and solid-to-liquid ratio on metal leaching was studied.
The relationship between the percentages of metals leached and the HCl concentration is shown in Fig. 1. The leaching of metals was found to depend highly on the HCl concentration at [ HCl ] < 2 mol l ^-1. Nearly complete dissolution occurred for all metals when the HCl concentration approached 3 mol 1 ^-1. However, there appeared to be a slight decrease in the percent of the rare earths leached when the HCl concentration exceeded 4 mol 1 ^-1
Fig. 2 illustrates that the leaching of iron is affected significantly by temperature. At low temperature, for instance, at 35 ^ ∘C, the percent leached could only reach about 40%, whereas this value would be increased with the increase in temperature, reaching completion at 95 ^ ∘C. It appears that the leach efficiency of nickel was less dependent on temperature at < 65 ^ ∘C, where the percent of nickel leached was kept at approximately 87 %. However, when the temperature was allowed to continue to rise, the leaching of nickel increased. Almost total dissolution was accomplished at 95 ^ ∘C.. The leaching of other metals was far less dependent on temperature over the temperature range examined. Essentially complete leaching could be achieved at 35 ^ ∘C for cobalt, rare earths and aluminum and at 55 ^ ∘C for zinc and manganese.
The time dependency of the leaching of metals with 2 M HCl solution at 95 ^ ∘C is given in Fig. 3. Apparently, the leaching of cobalt, aluminum, manganese and rare earths proceeded very rapidly, reaching completion in less than 15 min for aluminum and manganese and less than 30 min for cobalt and rare earths. On the other hand, the relatively slow leaching of iron, zinc and nickel, especially the latter, was observed. The complete leaching was achieved in about 1, 2 and 2.5 h for iron, zinc and nickel, respectively.
The effect of the weight of scrap on the leaching of metals is shown in Table 2 in terms of the percent recovery of metals in the leach liquor. Overall, low scrap weight gives high leaching yields of metals, whereas increasing the proportion of scrap leads to incomplete leaching, particularly nickel. The effect of scrap weight on leaching of rare earths seems to be insignificant within the experimental range of scrap weights studied. However, the use of excessively small amounts of scrap is evidently undesirable from the point of view of maximizing metal concentration in the leach liquor and minimizing the lixiviant consumption. Accordingly, the suitable scrap weight was considered to be 5.5 g in 50 ml of acid solution.
Based on the above experimental results, the final optimum conditions for leaching were determined to be 3 M hydrochloric acid, a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:9 at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C for 3 h. Under these conditions, 96% of nickel, > 99 % of rare earths and 100% of cobalt could be leached. At the same time, however, the other impurity elements were also nearly completely dissolved in the solution. The average composition of the resulting leach liquor was found to be approximately, in grams per liter: 23.4 Ni, 1.7 Co, 3.4 Fe, 0.72 Zn, 0.46 Al, 1.2 Mn, 4.2 La, 0.26 Ce, 0.82 Pr, 2.6 Nd Ž and 0.074 Sm total RE 7.95 gl ^-1). The chloride ion concentration was 50 g1 ^-1 and the pH was about 1.2.

## 3.3. RecoÕery of rare earths
3.3.1. Separation of impurities and rare earths from cobalt and nickel by solÕent extraction with D2EHPA
Investigations into the use of acidic organophosphorus reagents for the solvent extraction of metal ions from aqueous solutions have shown that D2EHPA in organic diluents can be highly loaded with divalent transition metals like Cu ^2+ [ 13 - 17 ], n ^2+ w x 13,16,17, Cd ^2+ w x 15,17, Zn ^2+ w x 2q w x 13,15–17, Co 13,14,16–18, Ni ^2+ 13,14,16,17.w x Moreover, the extractability sequence from chloride medium can be written as Zn ^2+ > Mn ^2+ > Cu ^2+ > Cd ^2+ ≈ C ^2+ > Ni ^2+ 13,17. D2EHPA also exhibits a powerful extrac-w x tion for trivalent metal cations like Fe ^3+ [ 19, 20 ] and Al ^3+ [ 21 - 23 ]. The pH1 / 2 values Ž. defined as the pH at which 50% metal extraction occurs for Zn ^2+, Mn ^2+, F⃗ ⃗e⃗ ⃗^⃗3⃗+⃗ 24, w x Al^3+ 25 lie below pH 3, whereas those of cobalt and nickel are 4.08 and 4.52 24,w x respectively. These data demonstrate the possibility of removing impurities from cobalt and nickel by the use of extraction with D2EHPA at low pH. On the other hand, it is well known that D2EHPA shows an excellent extraction behavior towards trivalent rare earth elements in weakly acidic solution 26,27, and undoubtedly still forms the basis of w x several commercial processes for the separation of these metals 28. Fortunately, thew x separation of the rare earths from these impurities can be achieved by means of selective precipitation with oxalic acid as will be described later.
Fig. 4 gives the results for the extraction of zinc, aluminum, iron, manganese, cobalt, nickel and rare earths with 25 vol.% D2EHPA in kerosene from the actual leach solution mentioned above at various pH values. It is clear that the rare earths can be quantitatively extracted and separated from cobalt and nickel at pH-2.2. However, as expected, under these conditions, nearly complete extraction of aluminum and iron as well as about 85% extraction of zinc takes place. Above pH 2.0, the extraction of cobalt begins to occur. It is noteworthy that, according to the reported data 12,17, manganesew x should be extracted to a considerable extent at pH close to 2. Nevertheless, it can be seen from Fig. 4 that a large amount of rare earths and other impurities such as iron, aluminum and zinc prevent manganese from being taken up into the organic phase, since D2EHPA can extract these metal ions more strongly than manganese. The resulting effect is that only a very small amount of manganese Ž.; 15% is transferred to the organic phase. Hence, it is necessary to increase the organic-to-aqueous ratio and use a multistage extraction operation in order to eliminate manganese completely from the solution. For this reason, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of manganese from the leach liquor by 25% D2EHPA in kerosene was constructed by contacting the two phases at various phase ratios at an equilibrium pH 2.0. The equilibrium data are presented in Fig. 5. The McCable–Thiele diagram indicates that essentially complete removal of manganese can be achieved in two counter-current stages at an organic-toaqueous phase ratio of 3:1. The aqueous feed liquor was therefore processed in a two-stage batch counter-current experiment over six cycles, using 240 ml of organic phase and 80 ml of aqueous phase for each contact. The equilibrium pH for each contact was adjusted to 2.0 with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. The raffinate obtained after a six-cycle operation, where steady-state conditions had been reached, showed the presence of 0.005 g l ^-1 of manganese. The concentrations of zinc and aluminum were, in g1 ^-1, 0.09 and 0.002, respectively, while those of iron and the rare earths were below
0.001 gl ^-1. The extraction of cobalt was less than 13%, whereas nickel was not extracted at all. The incomplete extraction of zinc is probably attributed to complexation of zinc ion with chloride ion 13,15,29.w x

text_chunk.text:
## 3.3. RecoÕery of rare earths
3.3.1. Separation of impurities and rare earths from cobalt and nickel by solÕent extraction with D2EHPA
Investigations into the use of acidic organophosphorus reagents for the solvent extraction of metal ions from aqueous solutions have shown that D2EHPA in organic diluents can be highly loaded with divalent transition metals like Cu ^2+ [ 13 - 17 ], n ^2+ w x 13,16,17, Cd ^2+ w x 15,17, Zn ^2+ w x 2q w x 13,15–17, Co 13,14,16–18, Ni ^2+ 13,14,16,17.w x Moreover, the extractability sequence from chloride medium can be written as Zn ^2+ > Mn ^2+ > Cu ^2+ > Cd ^2+ ≈ C ^2+ > Ni ^2+ 13,17. D2EHPA also exhibits a powerful extrac-w x tion for trivalent metal cations like Fe ^3+ [ 19, 20 ] and Al ^3+ [ 21 - 23 ]. The pH1 / 2 values Ž. defined as the pH at which 50% metal extraction occurs for Zn ^2+, Mn ^2+, F⃗ ⃗e⃗ ⃗^⃗3⃗+⃗ 24, w x Al^3+ 25 lie below pH 3, whereas those of cobalt and nickel are 4.08 and 4.52 24,w x respectively. These data demonstrate the possibility of removing impurities from cobalt and nickel by the use of extraction with D2EHPA at low pH. On the other hand, it is well known that D2EHPA shows an excellent extraction behavior towards trivalent rare earth elements in weakly acidic solution 26,27, and undoubtedly still forms the basis of w x several commercial processes for the separation of these metals 28. Fortunately, thew x separation of the rare earths from these impurities can be achieved by means of selective precipitation with oxalic acid as will be described later.
Fig. 4 gives the results for the extraction of zinc, aluminum, iron, manganese, cobalt, nickel and rare earths with 25 vol.% D2EHPA in kerosene from the actual leach solution mentioned above at various pH values. It is clear that the rare earths can be quantitatively extracted and separated from cobalt and nickel at pH-2.2. However, as expected, under these conditions, nearly complete extraction of aluminum and iron as well as about 85% extraction of zinc takes place. Above pH 2.0, the extraction of cobalt begins to occur. It is noteworthy that, according to the reported data 12,17, manganesew x should be extracted to a considerable extent at pH close to 2. Nevertheless, it can be seen from Fig. 4 that a large amount of rare earths and other impurities such as iron, aluminum and zinc prevent manganese from being taken up into the organic phase, since D2EHPA can extract these metal ions more strongly than manganese. The resulting effect is that only a very small amount of manganese Ž.; 15% is transferred to the organic phase. Hence, it is necessary to increase the organic-to-aqueous ratio and use a multistage extraction operation in order to eliminate manganese completely from the solution. For this reason, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of manganese from the leach liquor by 25% D2EHPA in kerosene was constructed by contacting the two phases at various phase ratios at an equilibrium pH 2.0. The equilibrium data are presented in Fig. 5. The McCable–Thiele diagram indicates that essentially complete removal of manganese can be achieved in two counter-current stages at an organic-toaqueous phase ratio of 3:1. The aqueous feed liquor was therefore processed in a two-stage batch counter-current experiment over six cycles, using 240 ml of organic phase and 80 ml of aqueous phase for each contact. The equilibrium pH for each contact was adjusted to 2.0 with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. The raffinate obtained after a six-cycle operation, where steady-state conditions had been reached, showed the presence of 0.005 g l ^-1 of manganese. The concentrations of zinc and aluminum were, in g1 ^-1, 0.09 and 0.002, respectively, while those of iron and the rare earths were below
0.001 gl ^-1. The extraction of cobalt was less than 13%, whereas nickel was not extracted at all. The incomplete extraction of zinc is probably attributed to complexation of zinc ion with chloride ion 13,15,29.w x

text_chunk.text:
## 3.3.2. Scrubbing of cobalt from the loaded organic phase
The small amount of cobalt co-extracted into the organic phase was easily removed by scrubbing with 0.3 M HCl solution at an O:A ratio of 22:1 in a single stage. The scrub solution contained, in gl ^-1, 1.70 Co, 1.63 Mn, 0.042 Zn, 0.010 Al and 0.013 La. No iron and none of the other rare earths was detected in the scrub solution. This solution was returned to be mixed with the leach liquor.

## 3.3.3. Stripping of rare earths
Additionally it can be seen from Table 3 that the stripping of iron is very poor under the experimental conditions. Nevertheless, further experiments showed that the stripping of iron was enhanced significantly when the concentration of hydrochloric acid exceeded 4 M. The McCable–Thiele plot Fig. 6 shows that a more than 99% stripping ofŽ. iron is theoretically possible using a 6 M HCl solution in four counter-current stages at an O:A ratio of 5:1. Under these conditions, aluminum is also removed completely from the organic phase.
After the stripping of iron, the organic phase is recycled to the extraction circuit for reuse.

text_chunk.text:
## 4. Recovery of cobalt and nickel
After removal of rare earths and impurities from the leach solution by extraction with D2EHPA, the remaining raffinate contained cobalt and nickel as well as a small amount of zinc. In order to recover pure cobalt and nickel products, a cobalt–nickel separation was required. It is known that the selective solvent extraction of cobalt from chloride solutions containing nickel using a tertiary amine extractant is being practiced on a commercial scale 30,31. The extraction of cobalt from an aqueous solution with loww x acidity rises with the chloride ion concentration. Substantial extraction of cobalt occurs at [ C ] ^- ] ≥200 g1 ^-1 32,33. Hence, in the present work, the raffinate was concentratedw x by evaporation to reach a chloride ion concentration of about 220 g1 ^-1 before extraction.
Preliminary tests on a concentrated aqueous feed liquor showed insufficient extraction of cobalt in a single contact at unit phase ratio with 25% TOA in kerosene. Accordingly, to achieve quantitative extraction of cobalt, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of cobalt from the concentrated solution by 25% TOA in kerosene was determined. The results are shown in Fig. 7. The McCable–Thiele construction demonstrates that it should be possible to achieve nearly complete extraction of cobalt from a solution initially containing 6.75 gl ^-1 of cobalt in three counter-current stages at an O:A ratio of 2:1. To confirm this, a three-stage counter-current batch simulation was carried out. After nine cycles the representative raffinate was found to contain 0.018 g 1 ^-1 of cobalt corresponding to an extraction yield of > 99.7 %. The loaded organic phase contained 3.37 g l ^-1 of cobalt.
Subsequently the cobalt in the loaded organic phase was stripped by contacting it with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution pH 2.0 in a single stage at an O:A ratio of 4:1. Ž. The stripped organic phase was found to contain only 0.007 g1 ^-1 of cobalt, indicating a stripping efficiency of 99.8%. The strip liquor was a pure cobalt chloride solution containing 13.45 gl ^-1 of cobalt. It should be pointed out, that although zinc has been reported to be extracted from chloride medium by TOA 32,34, no zinc was observed inw x the loaded organic phase in the current work.

text_chunk.text: The optimal operating conditions were found to be 3 M HCl at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C and a 3-h leach time, and it was possible to treat up to 5.5 g of scrap in 50 ml of acid solution where the recoveries 100% of cobalt, over 96% of nickel and 99% of rare earths were achieved. A mixed rare earth oxide of over 99% purity was obtained by selective precipitation with oxalic acid, and calcination of the precipitate. Nearly complete recovery of cobalt can be achieved by using a three-stage counter-current. extraction at an O:A ratio of 2:1, followed by stripping with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution Ž. pH 2.0 in a single stage at an O:A ratio of 4:1. A pure cobalt product and a nickel oxalate with a purity close to 99.9% were obtained.

process_stages.name: hydrochloric acid leaching of battery scrap
process_stages.evidence_hint: Leach tests on cells were carried out using hydrochloric acid solution. In each test, 3.08 g of battery scrap ... were leached in 50 ml of HCl solutions of suitable concentrations.

process_stages.name: solvent extraction with D2EHPA
process_stages.evidence_hint: Extraction and stripping tests were carried out batchwise by contacting suitable volumes of the organic and aqueous phases ... From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium.

process_stages.name: solvent extraction with TOA
process_stages.evidence_hint: The extraction and stripping kinetics of cobalt with TOA were very rapid. The time for reaching extraction equilibrium was less than 5 min, while the stripping occurred almost immediately after the loaded organic phase was contacted with a stripping agent.

process_stages.name: precipitation of rare earths
process_stages.evidence_hint: The mixed rare earths were precipitated from the strip liquors of the extraction circuit with D2EHPA by the addition of concentrated ammonia solution until a pH 2–3 was reached, followed by an excess of saturated oxalic acid solution about 2 mol rmol of rare earths. The mixture was heated and stirred for ca. 1 h, and the precipitated rare earth oxalate was filtered, washed with hot water, and dried in air. The oxalate was calcined in a muffle furnace at 850 - 900 °C to convert it to a mixed rare earth oxide product.

process_stages.name: precipitation of cobalt and nickel
process_stages.evidence_hint: The cobalt and nickel were precipitated from the strip liquor and the raffinate from extraction circuit with TOA, respectively, by the addition of ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions.

experiment_settings.name: hydrochloric acid leaching conditions
experiment_settings.stage_name: hydrochloric acid leaching of battery scrap

experiment_settings.name: solvent extraction with D2EHPA conditions
experiment_settings.condition_summary: batchwise; 50-ml centrifuge tube or 500-ml separatory funnel; ambient temperature (25 ± 0.5 °C); pH adjusted with concentrated NaOH; contact time 30 min for extraction and stripping equilibria except Al stripping ~60 min

From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium.

records.evidence_span: The Ni-MH batteries used in this work were cylinder-shaped batteries TOSHIBAŽ TH-3A type. The commercial extractants employed, bis 2-ethylhexyl phosphoric acid. Ž. Ž. Ž. D2EHPA was kindly donated by Daihachi Chemical Industry and trioctylamine TOA was purchased from Aldrich Chemical Company Inc. These reagents were utilized without any further purification. The concentrations of the extractants in the organic solution were 25% by volume. The diluent was kerosene. 1-Dodecanol was used as third phase inhibitor in the TOA system, and its concentration was 15 vol.%. The organic solution of TOA was pre-equilibrated by contacting with twice volume of 2 M hydrochloric acid solution for 10 min before the extraction experiments. Other reagents were of analytical reagent grade quality.

records.evidence_span: A completely hydrometallurgical process has been developed for the recovery of metal values such as cobalt, nickel and rare earths from spent nickel-metal hydride Ni-MH secondaryŽ. batteries. Effects of hydrochloric acid concentration, temperature, reaction time and solid-to-liquid ratio on leaching of metals contained in the electrode materials of the batteries were studied. The optimal operating conditions were found to be 3 M HCl at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C and a 3-h leach time, and it was possible to treat up to 5.5 g of scrap in 50 ml of acid solution where the recoveries 100% of cobalt, over 96% of nickel and 99% of rare earths were achieved. A typical chemical composition of the resulting leach liquor was approximately, in grams per liter, 23.4 Ni, 1.7 Co, 3.4 Fe, 0.72 Zn, 0.46 Al, 1.2 Mn, 4.2 La, 0.26 Ce, 0.82 Pr, 2.6 Nd and 0.074 Sm, as well as 50 Cl. The pH of the solution was around 1.2. The rare earth values can be readily recovered from the leach liquor by the use of a solvent extraction circuit with 25% bis 2-ethylhexylŽ. phosphoric acid D2EHPA in kerosene, in which a two-stage counter-current extraction at an O:A Ž. ratio of 3:1 at an equilibrium pH of 2.0, a single-stage cobalt scrubbing with 0.3 M hydrochloric acid at an O:A ratio of 22:1, and a stripping operation with 2.0 M hydrochloric acid in one contact at an O:A ratio of 5:1 are involved. A mixed rare earth oxide of over 99% purity was obtained by selective precipitation with oxalic acid, and calcination of the precipitate. The total yield of rare earths approached 98%. The cobalt and nickel in the raffinate are effectively separated by selective extraction of cobalt with 25% TOA in kerosene after concentration up to ClŽ w yxf220 g y1 l. Nearly complete recovery of cobalt can be achieved by using a three-stage counter-current.

records.scope_description: Precipitate mixed rare earths from D2EHPA strip liquors by adding concentrated ammonia solution to pH 2–3, then adding excess saturated oxalic acid solution (about 2 mol per mol of rare earths); heat and stir for about 1 h; filter, wash with hot water, dry in air, and calcine the oxalate in a muffle furnace at 850–900 °C to convert to mixed rare earth oxide product.

records.evidence_span: Leach tests on cells were carried out using hydrochloric acid solution. In each test, 3.08 g of battery scrap which consisted of 1.25 g of the positive electrode materials and 1.83 g of the negative electrode materials were leached in 50 ml of HCl solutions of suitable concentrations in a 100-ml beaker under electromagnetic stirring, except for the tests on the effect of solid-to-liquid ratio on the leaching of metals. After leaching, the leach solution and insoluble residue were separated by filtration. The concentrations of each metal in the leach solutions were measured.

records.evidence_span: Table 3 gives the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration and of organic-to-aqueous ratio on the stripping of metal ions from the organic phase. It was found that the rare earths could be stripped readily using a hydrochloric acid solution of appropriate concentration ca. 1–3 M. The somewhat low recoveries of rare earths at low HClŽ. concentration or at high O:A ratio are due to the incomplete stripping of praseodymium and neodymium from the organic phase. As expected, these rare earths are extracted by D2EHPA more strongly than the lighter rare earths like lanthanum and cerium. Almost quantitative stripping could be accomplished with 2 M HCl solution in a single contact at an O:A ratio of 5:1, thereby giving rise to a strip liquor containing, in gl ^-1, 13.2: RE 0.27 Al, 1.13 Zn, 1.72 Mn, 0.016 Co and 0.02 Fe. Higher concentrations of rare earths could be obtained, if required, by use of a multi-stage counter-current stripping operation at a greater O:A ratio.

records.evidence_span: The nickel-metal hydride batteries were cut in half longitudinally to separate the metallic cases from the internal battery rolls which consisted of the positive and negative electrodes plus a nylon separator. The cells weighed an average of 24.8 g each and contained an AB5 - t y p e rare earth metal system negative electrode. The weight of theŽ. positive electrode in one cell was 7.27 g and that of the negative electrode was 10.57 g in which the alloy powder accounted for 87.6% and the metal-mesh 12.4%. The components of the active material on the positive electrode, the alloy powder and the metal-mesh on the negative electrode were determined separately by total dissolution with aqua regia.

final.content: Leach 3.08 g of battery scrap (1.25 g positive electrode materials and 1.83 g negative electrode materials) in 50 mL of HCl solution of suitable concentration in a 100-mL beaker under electromagnetic stirring; after leaching, separate leach solution and insoluble residue by filtration.
final.evidence_span: Leach 3.08 g of battery scrap (1.25 g positive electrode materials and 1.83 g negative electrode materials) in 50 mL of HCl solution of suitable concentration in a 100-mL beaker under electromagnetic stirring; after leaching, separate leach solution and insoluble residue by filtration.

final.name: precipitation of cobalt and nickel
final.content: Precipitate cobalt from the TOA strip liquor and nickel from the TOA raffinate by adding ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions; dissolve the precipitates with small amounts of concentrated sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid solutions and dilute with water for impurity analysis.
final.evidence_span: Precipitate cobalt from the TOA strip liquor and nickel from the TOA raffinate by adding ammonium oxalate to the corresponding solutions; dissolve the precipitates with small amounts of concentrated sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid solutions and dilute with water for impurity analysis.

final.name: precipitation of rare earth
final.content: Precipitate mixed rare earths from D2EHPA strip liquors by adding concentrated ammonia solution to pH 2–3, then adding excess saturated oxalic acid solution (about 2 mol per mol of rare earths); heat and stir for about 1 h; filter, wash with hot water, dry in air, and calcine the oxalate in a muffle furnace at 850–900 °C to convert to mixed rare earth oxide product.
final.evidence_span: Precipitate mixed rare earths from D2EHPA strip liquors by adding concentrated ammonia solution to pH 2–3, then adding excess saturated oxalic acid solution (about 2 mol per mol of rare earths); heat and stir for about 1 h; filter, wash with hot water, dry in air, and calcine the oxalate in a muffle furnace at 850–900 °C to convert to mixed rare earth oxide product.

final.name: solvent extraction with D2EHPA
final.content: Batchwise extraction and stripping tests by contacting suitable volumes of organic and aqueous phases in a 50-mL centrifuge tube or 500-mL separatory funnel at 25 ± 0.5 °C; adjust pH with concentrated NaOH; use 30-min contact time for extraction and stripping equilibria of metal ions, except stripping of aluminum requires about 60 min.

final.name: solvent extraction with TOA
final.content: Batchwise extraction and stripping tests by contacting suitable volumes of organic and aqueous phases in a 50-mL centrifuge tube or 500-mL separatory funnel at 25 ± 0.5 °C; adjust pH with concentrated NaOH; extraction equilibrium for cobalt reached in less than 5 min and stripping occurs almost immediately after contacting loaded organic phase with stripping agent.

settings.condition_summary: batchwise; 50-ml centrifuge tube or 500-ml separatory funnel; ambient temperature (25 ± 0.5 °C); pH adjusted with concentrated NaOH; contact time 30 min for extraction and stripping equilibria except Al stripping ~60 min

condition_keys.raw_text: contact time 30 min for extraction and stripping equilibria except Al stripping ~60 min

settings.evidence_hint: Extraction and stripping tests were carried out batchwise by contacting suitable volumes of the organic and aqueous phases in a 50-ml centrifuge tube or a 500-ml separatory funnel at ambient temperature (25 ± 0.5 °C). The pH was adjusted by the addition of a concentrated sodium hydroxide solution to the appropriate value. From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium.

settings.evidence_hint: The mixed rare earths were precipitated from the strip liquors of the extraction circuit with D2EHPA by the addition of concentrated ammonia solution until a pH 2–3 was reached, followed by an excess of saturated oxalic acid solution about 2 mol rmol of rare earths. The mixture was heated and stirred for ca. 1 h, and the precipitated rare earth oxalate was filtered, washed with hot water, and dried in air. The oxalate was calcined in a muffle furnace at 850 - 900 °C to convert it to a mixed rare earth oxide product.
